source_evidence.anchor: equation (1.1) and the definitions immediately following it
source_evidence.observation: The one-dimensional transform uses the unnormalized positive-sign kernel exp(i 2 pi j k/N), takes complex input, distinguishes exact y from fl(y), and defines RMS as the square root of the mean squared magnitude.

The FFT is represented by permutation, block Fourier, and diagonal twiddle-factor matrices. The factorization applies to both Cooley-Tukey and Sande-Tukey variants with different diagonal matrices. Floating addition and multiplication satisfy Wilkinson-style first-order relative-error models with a machine-dependent epsilon and occurrence-dependent theta in [-1,1].

source_evidence.anchor: absolute sine/cosine error model and Theorem 1
source_evidence.observation: The paper introduces gamma >= 0 through absolute errors gamma theta epsilon in computed sines and cosines. Theorem 1 defines K(N,gamma) from the selected one-dimensional FFT radix factorization and gives the piecewise per-radix constant alpha.

source_evidence.anchor: first-order expansion in the proof of Theorem 1(a)
source_evidence.observation: After expanding products of factors 1+theta epsilon, the paper states that O(epsilon^2) includes all terms of order epsilon^2.
The one-dimensional FFT analysis assumes fl(x)=x; permutation matrices only reorder values and introduce no roundoff error.
The exact multidimensional transform is a product-indexed, unnormalized Fourier sum over s_1 through s_m, with s_l and t_l ranging from 0 to N_l-1 for l=1 through m.

The paper defines pointwise forward error E, multidimensional RMS and maximum errors, and states both parts of Theorem 2. Part (a) bounds relative RMS error by epsilon times the sum of the one-dimensional constants K(N_l,gamma), plus O(epsilon^2). Part (b) adds the square root of the total number of output entries for the maximum-error bound.

source_evidence.anchor: nested computation, telescoping decomposition, and equations (4.2)-(4.4)
source_evidence.observation: The exact intermediates satisfy Z_0=Y, Z_m=X, and Z_{l-1}=T_l Z_l. The computed nesting applies T_m first and T_1 last. The proof separates the total error into propagated local errors, invokes the one-dimensional local bound (4.3), and uses the exact scaling [Z_{l-1}]_RMS=sqrt(N_l)[Z_l]_RMS.

source_evidence.anchor: completion of the proof of Theorem 2(a)
source_evidence.observation: The propagated local terms have coefficients sqrt(N_1...N_l)K(N_l,gamma). Computed intermediate RMS values are replaced by their exact values plus O(epsilon), and exact intermediate norms scale from X by sqrt(N_{l+1}...N_m). The final step assumes the stored/computed input RMS equals the exact input RMS, or at least differs by O(epsilon).
Part (b) is obtained by the same RMS-to-maximum argument used for Theorem 1(b).

source_evidence.anchor: Conclusion paragraph on floating-point representation of input data
source_evidence.observation: The author states that the preceding analysis assumed input data exactly representable in machine precision. If input rounding is present, an additional error term is required; the page illustrates this for a one-dimensional input perturbation fl(x)=x+delta.

binders: The displayed result ranges over coordinate labels l=1,...,m and transform lengths N_l; each source and target index s_l,t_l ranges over 0,...,N_l-1 (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: equation (4.1)).

X(s_1,...,s_m) is the exact multidimensional input and Y(t_1,...,t_m) is its exact Fourier transform; fl(Y(t_1,...,t_m)) is the computed output component (PDF pp. 7-8, printed pp. 763-764, anchors: equation (4.1) and definition of E).

epsilon is a machine-dependent floating-point error constant, while every occurrence of theta may have a different value but satisfies -1 <= theta <= 1 (PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2) and following paragraph).

gamma is nonnegative, depends on how trigonometric values and their arguments are computed for a transform order, and is independent of the input data (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: absolute sine/cosine error model).

For each coordinate length N_l, K(N_l,gamma) is inherited from a chosen one-dimensional FFT factorization. If that factorization is disambiguatingly written N_l=product_{r=1}^{M_l} n_{l,r}, then K(N_l,gamma)=sum_{r=1}^{M_l} alpha(n_{l,r})+(M_l-1)(3+2 gamma) (PDF pp. 3 and 8, printed pp. 759 and 764, anchors: Theorem 1 and Theorem 2).
hypotheses: Y is computed by a multidimensional floating-point fast Fourier transform formed from nested one-dimensional transforms T_m through T_1 (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: nested computation in the proof of Theorem 2).

Real floating-point additions and multiplications obey equations (3.1)-(3.2), with no separate exceptional-case qualifications in those equations (PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equations (3.1)-(3.2)).

Computed sines and cosines obey the absolute-error model fl(sin(fl(a)))=sin(a)+gamma theta epsilon and fl(cos(fl(a)))=cos(a)+gamma theta epsilon (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: absolute sine/cosine error model).

The operational analysis assumes input data exactly representable in machine precision; the proof's final line also says equality of input RMS values, or a difference of O(epsilon), is sufficient for that step (PDF pp. 9 and 12, printed pp. 765 and 768, anchors: completion of Theorem 2(a) and Conclusion input-representation paragraph).

Each coordinate transform uses the one-dimensional FFT error constant corresponding to its actual radix factorization and separate twiddle-factor multiplications (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1 and its parenthetical radix formulas).
conclusions: Selected clause, Theorem 2(a): [fl(Y)-Y]_RMS/[Y]_RMS <= epsilon sum_{l=1}^m K(N_l,gamma)+O(epsilon^2) (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a)).

Sibling clause in the same multi-part theorem, Theorem 2(b): [fl(Y)-Y]_MAX/[Y]_RMS <= epsilon sqrt(N_1 N_2 ... N_m) sum_{l=1}^m K(N_l,gamma)+O(epsilon^2) (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(b)).
For each local coordinate transform, [fl(Z_{l-1})-Z_{l-1}]_RMS/[Z_l]_RMS <= epsilon sqrt(N_l)K(N_l,gamma)+O(epsilon^2) (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: equation (4.3)).
The exact coordinate transform scales RMS according to [Z_{l-1}]_RMS=sqrt(N_l)[Z_l]_RMS (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: equation (4.4)).

Before final simplification, the accumulated RMS error is bounded by epsilon times the sum over l of sqrt(product_{j=1}^l N_j)K(N_l,gamma)[fl(Z_l)]_RMS, with Z_m=X, plus O(epsilon^2) (PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: first displayed inequality completing Theorem 2(a)).
definitions_and_conventions: Equation (4.1) defines Y(t_1,...,t_m)=sum_{s_1}...sum_{s_m} e(s_1t_1/N_1+...+s_mt_m/N_m)X(s_1,...,s_m), with no normalization factor (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: equation (4.1)).
E(t_1,...,t_m)=fl(Y(t_1,...,t_m))-Y(t_1,...,t_m) is a forward error against the exact transform (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: definition of E).
[fl(Y)-Y]_RMS={sum_{t_1}...sum_{t_m}|E(t_1,...,t_m)|^2/(N_1...N_m)}^(1/2) (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: multidimensional RMS definition).
[fl(Y)-Y]_MAX=max_{t_1,...,t_m}|E(t_1,...,t_m)| (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: multidimensional maximum-error definition).
The denominator [Y]_RMS uses the same root-mean-square convention on the exact output Y (PDF pp. 1 and 8, printed pp. 757 and 764, anchors: RMS definition following equation (1.1) and Theorem 2).
Exact intermediate arrays satisfy Z_0=Y, Z_m=X, and Z_{l-1}=T_l Z_l for l=1,...,m (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: system following Theorem 2).
The piecewise one-dimensional constant is alpha(n)=sqrt(2) for n=2, alpha(n)=5 for n=4, and alpha(n)=2 sqrt(n)(n+gamma) otherwise (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: definition of alpha in Theorem 1).
implicit_context: The multidimensional arrays are complex-valued by inheritance from the paper's complex Fourier-transform setup; equation (1.1) explicitly declares complex input in the one-dimensional case (PDF pp. 1 and 7, printed pp. 757 and 763, anchors: equation (1.1) and equation (4.1)).
The transform is unnormalized and uses the positive exponential sign inherited from exp(i 2 pi j k/N) in equation (1.1) (PDF pp. 1 and 7, printed pp. 757 and 763, anchors: equations (1.1) and (4.1)).

Positive-integral m and N_l are operationally required by the finite index ranges, but the theorem does not separately state those quantifiers (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: index convention below equation (4.1)).

The bounds are deterministic worst-case roundoff bounds rather than statistical error estimates; theta is only constrained occurrence by occurrence to [-1,1] (PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: paragraph following equations (3.1)-(3.2)).
statement.algorithm_linkage: The proof computes fl(Y)=fl(T_1 fl(T_2 ... fl(T_m X)...)), so dimension m is transformed first and dimension 1 last, while exact intermediates obey Z_{l-1}=T_l Z_l (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: nested computation in the proof of Theorem 2). Each T_l invokes Theorem 1's one-dimensional floating-point FFT model, whose matrix factorization contains permutation matrices, radix-sized block Fourier matrices, and separate complex-diagonal twiddle-factor matrices (PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 758-759, anchors: equation (2.2) and Theorem 1). Equation (2.2) is stated to apply to both Cooley-Tukey and Sande-Tukey algorithms, with different diagonal matrices (PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: final algorithm remark before Section 3).
numerical_model: For floating-point a and b, fl(a+b)=a(1+theta epsilon)+b(1+theta epsilon), with generic theta occurrences independently allowed to vary within [-1,1] (PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equation (3.1) and following paragraph).
For floating-point a and b, fl(ab)=ab(1+theta epsilon), with |theta|<=1 (PDF p. 2, printed p. 758, anchor: equation (3.2) and following paragraph).

When sums use at least t+1 accumulator digits, epsilon=0.5 beta^(1-t) for rounded operations and epsilon=beta^(1-t) for chopped operations, where beta is the base and t the mantissa digit count (PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 758-759, anchor: paragraph spanning the page break after equations (3.1)-(3.2)).

When sums are accumulated with only t digits, epsilon=0.5(1+1/beta)beta^(1-t) for rounded operations and epsilon=(1+1/beta)beta^(1-t) for chopped operations (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: continuation of the epsilon definition).

Trigonometric values use an absolute, not relative, error model: both the rounded argument and the computed sine or cosine are covered by an additive gamma theta epsilon term (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: absolute sine/cosine error model).
Permutation stages are treated as exact reorderings and introduce no roundoff (PDF p. 5, printed p. 761, anchor: discussion preceding equation (3.6)).
error_notions: The selected result is a normwise relative forward-error bound: computed multidimensional output minus exact multidimensional Fourier output, measured in RMS and divided by exact-output RMS (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchors: definition of E and Theorem 2(a)).

The sibling part is a maximum absolute componentwise output error divided by exact-output RMS; it is not divided by a maximum norm (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchors: maximum-error definition and Theorem 2(b)).
The theorem does not claim a componentwise relative-error bound, a backward-error bound, or a probabilistic mean-square estimate (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2).

The total forward error is decomposed into local roundoff from each coordinate transform propagated through all earlier exact transforms (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchors: telescoping identity and equation (4.2)).
norms: For an array over N_1...N_m entries, RMS is the Euclidean magnitude divided by sqrt(N_1...N_m) (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: multidimensional RMS definition).
MAX is the largest complex magnitude over all product indices (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: multidimensional maximum-error definition).
The unnormalized one-coordinate Fourier map multiplies RMS by sqrt(N_l), exactly as stated in equation (4.4) (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: equation (4.4)).
Consequently, [Z_l]_RMS=sqrt(N_{l+1}...N_m)[X]_RMS for the exact intermediates used in the proof (PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: norm substitution completing Theorem 2(a)).
constants_and_indexing: All source and target coordinate indices are zero-based: s_l,t_l=0,1,...,N_l-1 for l=1,...,m (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: index convention below equation (4.1)).
For a one-dimensional factorization N=product_{r=1}^M n_r, K(N,gamma)=sum_{r=1}^M alpha(n_r)+(M-1)(3+2 gamma) (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: definition of K in Theorem 1).
For radix 2, K(2^M,gamma)=(3+sqrt(2)+2 gamma)M-(3+2 gamma); for radix 4, K(4^M,gamma)=(8+2 gamma)M-(3+2 gamma) (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: parenthetical special cases after Theorem 1).
The K constants include separate multiplications by the diagonal twiddle matrices D_r for r=1,...,M-1 (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: sentence following the radix-2 and radix-4 formulas).
Theorem 2 sums one K(N_l,gamma) for every coordinate l, without an additional dimension-dependent coefficient in the relative RMS conclusion (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a)).
higher_order_terms: The stated result retains the first-order term epsilon sum_l K(N_l,gamma) and appends O(epsilon^2) (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a)).

In the one-dimensional derivation, O(epsilon^2) is said to include all terms of order epsilon^2 arising from expansion of the roundoff factors (PDF p. 4, printed p. 760, anchor: first-order expansion in the proof of Theorem 1(a)).

The multidimensional proof uses [fl(Z_l)]_RMS=[Z_l]_RMS+O(epsilon) for l=1,...,m-1, so multiplying those first-order norm perturbations by epsilon contributes only to O(epsilon^2) (PDF p. 9, printed p. 765, anchor: completion of Theorem 2(a)).

No explicit coefficient, uniformity domain, or threshold for the O(epsilon^2) remainder is supplied (PDF pp. 4 and 8-9, printed pp. 760 and 764-765, anchors: definition of O(epsilon^2) and proof of Theorem 2(a)).
exceptional_values: The relative RMS expressions require [Y]_RMS to be nonzero to be ordinary real-valued ratios, but the theorem does not state [Y]_RMS>0 or handle the zero-output case separately (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2).

The rounding model contains no explicit treatment of overflow, underflow, subnormal values, infinities, NaNs, or failed trigonometric evaluation (PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 758-759, anchors: equations (3.1)-(3.2) and trigonometric error model).

Input-representation error is excluded from the preceding analysis by the exact-representability assumption; the paper says a separate term must be added when fl(X) differs from X (PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: Conclusion input-representation paragraph).

undebatable_constraints: The selected bound is relative RMS forward error, not absolute RMS error: its denominator is the RMS of exact Y (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a)).
Its first-order coefficient is exactly sum_{l=1}^m K(N_l,gamma), with no factor sqrt(N_1...N_m) in part (a) (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a)).
The square-root total-size factor sqrt(N_1...N_m) belongs to the sibling maximum-error bound in part (b) (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(b)).
The exact transform is product-indexed with zero-based ranges s_l,t_l=0,...,N_l-1 (PDF p. 7, printed p. 763, anchor: equation (4.1) and its index convention).
The transform is unnormalized; the exact one-coordinate RMS scaling is sqrt(N_l) (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: equation (4.4)).
The computation is explicitly nested as T_m first through T_1 last (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: displayed nested computation).
Each K(N_l,gamma) must be the Theorem 1 constant for the actual one-dimensional radix factorization used in coordinate l (PDF pp. 3 and 8, printed pp. 759 and 764, anchors: Theorem 1 and Theorem 2).
The alpha cases n=2, n=4, and otherwise are distinct and must be preserved (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: piecewise definition of alpha).
The analysis includes roundoff in trigonometric values through an absolute gamma theta epsilon model (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: sine/cosine error model).
The result is first-order and explicitly includes an O(epsilon^2) remainder (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(a)).
The exact-input scope cannot be silently replaced by arbitrary rounded input without adding an input-error contribution (PDF p. 12, printed p. 768, anchor: Conclusion input-representation paragraph).

The telescoping proof propagates every coordinate's local error; no coordinate term may be omitted from the sum (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp. 764-765, anchors: equation (4.2) and the accumulated inequality).

ambiguities.issue: The shorthand e(q) in equation (4.1) is not separately defined on the cited multidimensional pages.
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (4.1) literally writes e(s_1t_1/N_1+...+s_mt_m/N_m), while equation (1.1) writes the one-dimensional kernel explicitly as exp(i 2 pi j k/N) (PDF pp. 1 and 7, printed pp. 757 and 763, anchors: equations (1.1) and (4.1)).
ambiguities.impact: Interpreting e(q) as exp(i 2 pi q) is strongly inherited from the Fourier context, but a formal contract should mark that identification as inherited rather than as a standalone definition on page 763 (PDF pp. 1 and 7, anchors: equations (1.1) and (4.1)).

ambiguities.issue: The notation K(N,gamma) suppresses dependence on the selected radix factorization and therefore is not determined by N alone.
ambiguities.evidence: Theorem 1 assumes N=N_1...N_M and defines K using every factor N_l, while Theorem 2 merely refers to K(N_l,gamma) as the error constant from Theorem 1 (PDF pp. 3 and 8, printed pp. 759 and 764, anchors: Theorems 1 and 2).
ambiguities.impact: A formal statement must bind the one-dimensional factor list or the concrete FFT algorithm for each coordinate; treating K as a factorization-independent function of N_l would lose source information (PDF p. 3, anchor: definition of K).

ambiguities.issue: The paper uses one symbol gamma in Theorem 2 even though gamma was described as depending on computation for a transform of a given order.
ambiguities.evidence: The trigonometric-model paragraph says gamma depends on how sines, cosines, and their arguments are computed for a transformation of a given order, whereas Theorem 2 writes K(N_l,gamma) with the same gamma for every l (PDF pp. 3 and 8, printed pp. 759 and 764, anchors: trigonometric error model and Theorem 2).
ambiguities.impact: For dimensions of different orders, the text does not say whether gamma is a common worst-case bound or whether dimension-specific constants have been collapsed into one symbol (PDF pp. 3 and 8, anchors: trigonometric model and Theorem 2).

ambiguities.issue: The exact-input scope and the weaker final proof condition are not stated identically.
ambiguities.evidence: The proof concludes by assuming equality of computed and exact input RMS values, or at least a difference of O(epsilon), while the Conclusion says the preceding analysis assumed every input number exactly representable in machine precision (PDF pp. 9 and 12, printed pp. 765 and 768, anchors: completion of Theorem 2(a) and Conclusion input-representation paragraph).
ambiguities.impact: The conservative operational contract is exact representability. The weaker RMS-only condition should not be generalized into an arbitrary componentwise input-perturbation allowance, because the paper says nonexact input requires an additional error term (PDF p. 12, anchor: input-representation paragraph).

ambiguities.issue: The theorem does not address a zero exact-output RMS denominator.
ambiguities.evidence: Both parts divide by [Y]_RMS, but no hypothesis [Y]_RMS>0 and no zero case appears in the theorem statement (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2).
ambiguities.impact: A formal ratio theorem must either assume [Y]_RMS>0, use a division convention, or state a non-relative equivalent; the source does not choose among these options (PDF p. 8, anchor: Theorem 2).

ambiguities.issue: The asymptotic meaning and uniformity of O(epsilon^2) are not quantified.
ambiguities.evidence: The proof says O(epsilon^2) includes terms of order epsilon^2, but supplies no bound constant, epsilon range, or uniformity statement over dimensions, data, or radix choices (PDF pp. 4 and 8-9, printed pp. 760 and 764-765, anchors: first-order expansion and Theorem 2 proof).
ambiguities.impact: The source supports a first-order asymptotic claim, not a fully quantified finite-epsilon remainder estimate (PDF pp. 4 and 8, anchors: O(epsilon^2) explanation and Theorem 2(a)).

ambiguities.issue: The theorem names a multidimensional FFT but does not select uniquely between the Cooley-Tukey and Sande-Tukey one-dimensional variants.
ambiguities.evidence: The matrix factorization is stated to hold for both variants with different diagonal matrices, and Theorem 2 inherits Theorem 1 without naming one variant (PDF pp. 2 and 8, printed pp. 758 and 764, anchors: algorithm remark after equation (2.2) and Theorem 2).
ambiguities.impact: The contract covers implementations satisfying the inherited factorization and error constants; it should not assert a unique twiddle schedule beyond the explicitly displayed coordinate nesting (PDF pp. 2 and 8, anchors: equation (2.2) remarks and nested computation).

ambiguities.issue: Exceptional floating-point behavior is outside the stated model.
ambiguities.evidence: Equations (3.1)-(3.2) and the trigonometric model contain only bounded theta errors and do not discuss overflow, underflow, subnormals, infinities, or NaNs (PDF pp. 2-3, printed pp. 758-759, anchors: floating arithmetic and trigonometric models).
ambiguities.impact: Any formalization using IEEE exceptional values needs additional assumptions excluding them; those assumptions are not explicitly supplied by the paper (PDF pp. 2-3, anchors: equations (3.1)-(3.2) and trigonometric model).

contract_plain_english: For the product-indexed, unnormalized complex Fourier transform in equation (4.1), compute the dimensions sequentially by floating-point one-dimensional FFTs, applying dimension m first and dimension 1 last (PDF pp. 7-8, printed pp. 763-764, anchors: equation (4.1) and nested computation). Under the paper's bounded floating addition, multiplication, and absolute trigonometric-error models, and within its exact-input scope, the RMS forward error divided by the RMS of the exact output is at most epsilon times the sum of the one-dimensional constants K(N_l,gamma), up to O(epsilon^2) (PDF pp. 2-3, 8, and 12, printed pp. 758-759, 764, and 768, anchors: equations (3.1)-(3.2), trigonometric model, Theorem 2(a), and input-representation paragraph). Each K must retain the radix-factorization-dependent definition from Theorem 1 (PDF p. 3, printed p. 759, anchor: Theorem 1). The enclosing theorem also bounds maximum output error divided by exact-output RMS by the same sum multiplied by sqrt(N_1...N_m) (PDF p. 8, printed p. 764, anchor: Theorem 2(b)).
